claim: More than 90% of lung cancers are caused by cigarette smoke and air pollution, with polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) as key carcinogens.
source: More than 90% of lung cancers are caused by cigarette smoke and air pollution, with polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) as key carcinogens.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about lung cancer etiology.

claim: In Xuanwei City of Yunnan Province, the lung cancer incidence is among the highest in China, attributed to smoky coal combustion-generated PAH pollution.
source: In Xuanwei City of Yunnan Province, the lung cancer incidence is among the highest in China, attributed to smoky coal combustion-generated PAH pollution.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on Xuanwei lung cancer epidemiology.

claim: CXCL13 was overexpressed in 63/70 (90%) of Xuanwei NSCLCs.
source: we screened for abnormal inflammatory factors in non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLCs) from Xuanwei and control regions (CR) where smoky coal was not used, and found that a chemokine CXCL13 was overexpressed in 63/70 (90%) of Xuanwei NSCLCs
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study's screening of inflammatory factors in patient samples.

claim: CXCL13 was overexpressed in 44/71 (62%) of smoker CR patients.
source: and found that a chemokine CXCL13 was overexpressed in 63/70 (90%) of Xuanwei NSCLCs and 44/71 (62%) of smoker and 27/60 (45%) of non-smoker CR patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study's analysis of control region patient samples.

claim: CXCL13 was overexpressed in 27/60 (45%) of non-smoker CR patients.
source: and found that a chemokine CXCL13 was overexpressed in 63/70 (90%) of Xuanwei NSCLCs and 44/71 (62%) of smoker and 27/60 (45%) of non-smoker CR patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study's analysis of control region patient samples.

claim: CXCL13 overexpression was associated with the region Xuanwei and cigarette smoke.
source: CXCL13 overexpression was associated with the region Xuanwei and cigarette smoke.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the patient data showing associations between CXCL13 expression and these factors.

claim: Benzo(a)pyrene (BaP) induced CXCL13 production in lung epithelial cells.
source: The key carcinogen benzo(a)pyrene (BaP) induced CXCL13 production in lung epithelial cells and in mice prior to development of detectable lung cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro cell culture experiments with BaP treatment.

claim: BaP induced CXCL13 production in mice prior to development of detectable lung cancer.
source: The key carcinogen benzo(a)pyrene (BaP) induced CXCL13 production in lung epithelial cells and in mice prior to development of detectable lung cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse studies showing elevated CXCL13 before tumor detection.

claim: Deficiency in Cxcl13 significantly attenuated BaP-induced lung cancer in mice.
source: Deficiency in Cxcl13 or its receptor, Cxcr5, significantly attenuated BaP-induced lung cancer in mice, demonstrating CXCL13's critical role in PAH-induced lung carcinogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Cxcl13 knockout mouse studies.

claim: Deficiency in Cxcr5 significantly attenuated BaP-induced lung cancer in mice.
source: Deficiency in Cxcl13 or its receptor, Cxcr5, significantly attenuated BaP-induced lung cancer in mice, demonstrating CXCL13's critical role in PAH-induced lung carcinogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Cxcr5 knockout mouse studies.

claim: CXCL13 plays a critical role in PAH-induced lung carcinogenesis.
source: Deficiency in Cxcl13 or its receptor, Cxcr5, significantly attenuated BaP-induced lung cancer in mice, demonstrating CXCL13's critical role in PAH-induced lung carcinogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the knockout mouse experimental data showing reduced tumor burden.

claim: Air pollution is a diverse mixture of pollutants including particulate matter (PM), gases, organic compounds, metals, and microbes.
source: Air pollution is a diverse mixture of pollutants that originated from anthropogenic and natural sources, is comprised of particulate matter (PM), gases (e.g., sulfur oxides, carbon monoxide, ozone), organic compounds (e.g., polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, PAHs), metals (e.g., lead, vanadium, and nickel), and others, such as microbes (Akimoto, 2003; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on air pollution composition.

claim: 80% of the global population resides in locations where the ambient pollutant concentrations exceed the WHO Air Quality Guideline.
source: satellite observations suggest that 80% of the global population resides in locations where the ambient pollutant concentrations exceed the World Health Organization (WHO) Air Quality Guideline (van Donkelaar et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to satellite observation data.

claim: Outdoor air pollution was estimated to cause 3.7 million premature deaths annually worldwide in 2012, including 220,000 deaths due to lung cancer.
source: Outdoor air pollution in cities and rural areas was estimated to cause 3.7 million premature deaths annually worldwide in 2012, including 220,000 deaths due to lung cancer (WHO, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to WHO data.

claim: Outdoor air pollution has been classified as a Group 1 carcinogen in humans by the IARC.
source: Recently, outdoor (Loomis et al., 2013) and indoor (WHO, 2010) air pollution has been classified as a Group 1 carcinogen in humans by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) of WHO.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to IARC classification.

claim: Indoor air pollution has been classified as a Group 1 carcinogen in humans by the IARC.
source: Recently, outdoor (Loomis et al., 2013) and indoor (WHO, 2010) air pollution has been classified as a Group 1 carcinogen in humans by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) of WHO.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to IARC classification.

claim: The risk of lung cancer rises by 18% for every increase of 5 μg/m3 of PM2.5 in the environment.
source: Indeed, the risk of lung cancer rises by 18% for every increase of 5 μg/m3 of PM smaller than 2.5 μm in diameter (PM2.5) in the environment; the risk increases by 22% for every increase of 10 μg/m3 in PM smaller than 10 μm (PM10) (Raaschou-Nielsen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to epidemiological research.

claim: The risk of lung cancer increases by 22% for every increase of 10 μg/m3 in PM10.
source: Indeed, the risk of lung cancer rises by 18% for every increase of 5 μg/m3 of PM smaller than 2.5 μm in diameter (PM2.5) in the environment; the risk increases by 22% for every increase of 10 μg/m3 in PM smaller than 10 μm (PM10) (Raaschou-Nielsen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to epidemiological research.

claim: Until the 1970s, residents of Xuanwei used smoky coal in unvented indoor fire pits for domestic cooking and heating.
source: Until the 1970s, residents of this region used smoky coal in unvented indoor fire pits for domestic cooking and heating, which are processes that release high concentrations of PM2.5/PM10 that contain high concentration PAHs (Mumford et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to historical research on Xuanwei.

claim: Smoky coal combustion in Xuanwei releases high concentrations of PM2.5/PM10 that contain high concentration PAHs.
source: Until the 1970s, residents of this region used smoky coal in unvented indoor fire pits for domestic cooking and heating, which are processes that release high concentrations of PM2.5/PM10 that contain high concentration PAHs (Mumford et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to research on Xuanwei air pollution.

claim: Indoor air pollution in Xuanwei is associated with a significant increase in the absolute lifetime risk of developing lung cancer.
source: Indoor air pollution in Xuanwei is associated with a significant increase in the absolute lifetime risk of developing lung cancer (Xiao et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to epidemiological research.

claim: In Xuanwei, the male-to-female ratio of lung cancer incidences is 1.09:1.
source: In Xuanwei, the male-to-female ratio of lung cancer incidences is 1.09:1, while that of China's national average reaches 2.08:1 (Xiao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to epidemiological data.

claim: China's national average male-to-female ratio of lung cancer incidences is 2.08:1.
source: In Xuanwei, the male-to-female ratio of lung cancer incidences is 1.09:1, while that of China's national average reaches 2.08:1 (Xiao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to epidemiological data.

claim: Tobacco smoke was weakly and non-significantly associated with lung cancer risk in Xuanwei.
source: Tobacco smoke was weakly and non-significantly associated with lung cancer risk in this region (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to epidemiological research.

claim: In the 1990s, a reduction in the lung cancer incidence was noted after stove improvement in Xuanwei.
source: In the 1990s, a reduction in the lung cancer incidence was noted after stove improvement, supporting the association between indoor air pollution and lung cancer (Lan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to intervention study data.

claim: Lung cancer incidence in Xuanwei is still increasing.
source: However, lung cancer incidence in Xuanwei is still increasing (Li et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent epidemiological data.

claim: The key carcinogens of smoky coal combustion are PAHs.
source: Furthermore, the key carcinogens of smoky coal combustion are PAHs (Lv et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to research on coal combustion carcinogens.

claim: PAHs are the key carcinogens of tobacco smoke that causes more than 85% of global lung cancer deaths.
source: which are also the key carcinogens of tobacco smoke that causes more than 85% of global lung cancer deaths (Hecht, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to research on tobacco smoke carcinogens.

claim: Chronic inflammation can promote cancer formation, progression and metastasis by inducing oncogenic mutations, genomic instability, and enhanced angiogenesis.
source: Chronic inflammation can promote cancer formation, progression and metastasis by inducing oncogenic mutations, genomic instability, and enhanced angiogenesis (Grivennikov et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to research on inflammation and cancer.

claim: PAHs can cause immune suppression.
source: Studies show that PAHs can cause immune suppression (Zaccaria and McClure, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to research on PAH immunological effects.

claim: PAHs induce the secretion of cytokines/chemokines, including TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, CCL1, CXCL1, and CXCL5.
source: and induce the secretion of cytokines/chemokines, including tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, IL-8, CC chemokine ligand 1 (CCL1), chemokine (C-X-C motif) ligand 1 (CXCL1), and CXCL5 (N'Diaye et al., 2006; Umannová et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012; Dreij et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on PAH-induced cytokine production.

claim: Using a microarray analysis of 84 cytokines/chemokines in eight HPR NSCLCs, the expression of four cytokines (IL-1F5, IL-1F9, MIF, and SPP1) and seven chemokines (CXCL13, CCL7, CCL20, CCL26, CXCL6, CXCL9, and CXCL14) was increased in tumors compared with their counterpart normal lung tissues.
source: Using a microarray analysis of 84 cytokines/chemokines in tumor samples and their adjacent normal lung tissues of eight HPR NSCLCs, we found that the expression of four cytokines (IL-1F5, IL-1F9, MIF, and SPP1) and seven chemokines (CXCL13, CCL7, CCL20, CCL26, CXCL6, CXCL9, and CXCL14) was increased in tumors compared with their counterpart normal lung tissues (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental microarray data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CXCL13 was the most significantly up-regulated gene among the inflammatory factors, with an average of 63-fold higher expression in the tumor samples than in the normal controls.
source: Among them, CXCL13 was the most significantly up-regulated gene, with an average of 63-fold (10.48–173.65) higher expression in the tumor samples than in the normal controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental microarray data analysis.

claim: The expression of three cytokines (IL-1α, IL-5, and TNF-α) and nine chemokines (CCL4, CCL17, CCL18, CCL21, CCL23, CXCL1, CXCL2, CXCL3, and CXCL5) was lower in the tumor samples than in the normal controls.
source: The expression of three cytokines (IL-1α, IL-5, and TNF-α) and nine chemokines (CCL4, CCL17, CCL18, CCL21, CCL23, CXCL1, CXCL2, CXCL3, and CXCL5) was lower in the tumor samples than in the normal controls (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental microarray data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CXCL13 expression was elevated in the tumor tissues from 63/70 (90%) HPR patients compared with their normal controls.
source: We expanded these observations, and found that the expression of CXCL13 was elevated in the tumor tissues from 63/70 (90%) HPR patients (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CXCL13 expression was elevated in 71/131 (54.2%) CR patients compared with their normal controls.
source: and 71/131 (54.2%) CR patients (Table 1) compared with their normal controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Table 1.

claim: CXCL13 expression was much higher in the HPR patients than the CR cases (p<0.002).
source: CXCL13 expression was much higher in the HPR patients than the CR cases (p<0.002; Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The expression of the CXCL13 protein was significantly higher in the tumor samples than their adjacent normal controls.
source: Using immunohistochemistry (IHC) and immunoreactivity scoring, we showed that the expression of the CXCL13 protein was significantly higher in the tumor samples than their adjacent normal controls (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: CXCL13 expression was higher in the HPR NSCLCs than the CR patients.
source: CXCL13 expression was higher in the HPR NSCLCs than the CR patients, and the CR smoker NSCLCs had higher CXCL13 levels than the CR non-smoker patients (Figure 1B, D, E, and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures and Table 1.

claim: CR smoker NSCLCs had higher CXCL13 levels than the CR non-smoker patients.
source: CXCL13 expression was higher in the HPR NSCLCs than the CR patients, and the CR smoker NSCLCs had higher CXCL13 levels than the CR non-smoker patients (Figure 1B, D, E, and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures and Table 1.

claim: CXCL13 was much higher in the tumor samples than their adjacent normal lung tissues as shown by Western blot.
source: Using Western blot assays, we found that CXCL13 was much higher in the tumor samples than their adjacent normal lung tissues (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The CXCL13 serum concentration was higher in the HPR patients compared with the CR patients.
source: ELISA showed that the CXCL13 serum concentration was higher in the HPR patients compared with the CR patients, while the latter was higher than the healthy donors (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The CXCL13 serum concentration in CR patients was higher than in healthy donors.
source: ELISA showed that the CXCL13 serum concentration was higher in the HPR patients compared with the CR patients, while the latter was higher than the healthy donors (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In HPR, smoker and non-smoker NSCLCs had approximately equal expression levels of CXCL13 (p=0.17).
source: CXCL13 expression was not significantly different in smoker and non-smoker HPR patients (p=0.17; Table 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of patient data in Table 1.

claim: In NSCLCs from CRs, the expression of CXCL13 was significantly higher in smokers (44/71, 62%) than in non-smokers (27/60, 45%, p=0.04).
source: In NSCLCs from CRs, however, the expression of CXCL13 was significantly higher in smokers (44/71, 62%) than in non-smokers (27/60, 45%, p=0.04; Table 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of patient data in Table 1.

claim: Among the 201 NSCLCs, CXCL13-high was associated with HPR (p=4.6×10–6).
source: The multivariate logistic analyses showed that among the 201 NSCLCs, CXCL13-high was associated with HPR (p=4.6×10–6) and tobacco smoke (p=0.032; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate logistic analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: Among the 201 NSCLCs, CXCL13-high was associated with tobacco smoke (p=0.032).
source: The multivariate logistic analyses showed that among the 201 NSCLCs, CXCL13-high was associated with HPR (p=4.6×10–6) and tobacco smoke (p=0.032; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate logistic analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: Patients of both HPR and CR regions with relatively earlier disease (stages I and II) had lower CXCL13, while those with advanced disease (stages III and IV) had higher CXCL13.
source: We showed patients of both HPR and CR regions with relatively earlier disease (stages I and II) had lower CXCL13, while those with advanced disease (stages III and IV) had higher CXCL13 (Figure 1K)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: CXCL13-high was associated with TNM stage (p=0.003).
source: and multivariate logistic analyses showed that CXCL13-high was associated with TNM stage (Table 2, p=0.003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate logistic analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: In 54 CR patients, the median survival time of CXCL13-high patients (965 days) was much shorter than the CXCL13-low cases (1193 days, p=0.03).
source: In 54 CR patients whose survival information was available (Table 3), the median survival time of CXCL13-high patients (965 days) was much shorter than the CXCL13-low cases (1193 days, p=0.03; Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 1L and Table 3.

claim: BaP treatment of 16HBE cells at 1 μM for 30 days resulted in CXCL13 being the most significantly up-regulated gene among the 84 cytokines/chemokines.
source: To test the effects of PAHs on cytokine/chemokine production, the normal human lung epithelial 16HBE cells (Cozens et al., 1994) were exposed to a representative PAH compound benzo(a)pyrene (BaP) at 1 μM for a long period of time (30 days). We found that CXCL13 was the most significantly up-regulated gene among the 84 cytokines/chemokines (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray data from BaP-treated cells shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BaP up-regulated CXCL13 at both the mRNA and protein levels in a dose- and time-dependent manner in 16HBE and A549 lung cancer cells.
source: We confirmed that BaP up-regulated CXCL13 at both the mRNA and protein levels in a dose- and time-dependent manner in 16HBE and A549 lung cancer cells (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR and ELISA data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: All BaP-treated A/J mice developed lung cancer within 6 months.
source: All BaP-treated animals developed lung cancer within 6 months, as detected by a microCT scan (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C) and histopathology (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by microCT and histopathology data shown in the figures.

claim: Cxcl13 was significantly up-regulated in the tumor samples compared with their normal counterparts at both the mRNA and protein levels in BaP-treated mice.
source: We found that Cxcl13 was significantly up-regulated in the tumor samples compared with their normal counterparts at both the mRNA (Figure 2E) and protein (Figure 2D) levels
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR and IHC data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Cxcl13 serum concentrations increased in BaP-treated mice.
source: which paralleled the increase in Cxcl13 serum concentrations (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: BaP increased Cxcl13 concentrations in peripheral blood of the mice at 1 month after the beginning of the treatment, at which point no tumors were observed.
source: Notably, BaP increased Cxcl13 concentrations in peripheral blood of the mice at 1 month after the beginning of the treatment (Figure 2F), at which point no tumors were observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data and histopathology shown in the figures.

claim: Both Ttf1-positive lung cancer cells and Cd68-positive macrophages were stained positive for Cxcl13 in mouse lung tumor tissues.
source: By IHC assay, we found that both the Ttf1-positive lung cancer cells and Cd68-positive macrophages were stained positive for Cxcl13, but Ttf1-positive cells constituted more than 95% of the cellular component of the lung tumor tissues of the mice (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Ttf1-positive cells constituted more than 95% of the cellular component of the lung tumor tissues of BaP-treated mice.
source: By IHC assay, we found that both the Ttf1-positive lung cancer cells and Cd68-positive macrophages were stained positive for Cxcl13, but Ttf1-positive cells constituted more than 95% of the cellular component of the lung tumor tissues of the mice (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Ttf1 positive lung cancer cells were the main source of Cxcl13 in mice exposed to BaP.
source: These results indicate that Ttf1 positive lung cancer cells were the main source of Cxcl13 in mice exposed to BaP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the IHC and immunofluorescence data showing predominant Cxcl13 expression in Ttf1-positive cells.

claim: Dexamethasone (DEX) down-regulated Cxcl13 mRNA and protein, and reduced the Cxcl13 serum concentration in BaP-treated mice.
source: We further showed that the anti-inflammatory drug dexamethasone (DEX) (Wattenberg and Estensen, 1996) down-regulated Cxcl13 mRNA and protein, and reduced the Cxcl13 serum concentration (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR, IHC, and ELISA data shown in Figures 2D-F.

claim: DEX reduced the tumor burden in BaP-treated mice.
source: DEX reduced the tumor burden (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C, Figure 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by microCT and histopathology data shown in the figures.

claim: DEX prolonged the survival of BaP-treated mice.
source: and prolonged the survival (Figure 2I) of the mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Cxcl12 was not significantly changed in the BaP-treated mice.
source: Cxcl12, which was shown to be associated with lung cancer (Teicher and Fricker, 2010), was not significantly changed in the BaP-treated mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A potential XRE-like sequence, 5'-GCCCAGGCTGGAGTGCAG-3', is located at 1.7 kb downstream from the CXCL13 transcription start site.
source: The potential XRE-like sequence, 5'-GCCCAGGCTGGAGTGCAG-3', is located at 1.7 kb downstream from the transcription start site (TSS; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AhR could not bind CXCL13 in A549 cells without BaP treatment.
source: The potential interaction between AhR and CXCL13 was analyzed by the chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay, and the results showed that AhR could not bind CXCL13 in A549 cells without BaP treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP assay data.

claim: AhR-CXCL13 interaction was detected and CXCL13 was significantly up-regulated in the presence of BaP.
source: Interestingly, AhR-CXCL13 interaction was detected and CXCL13 was significantly up-regulated in the presence of BaP, revealed by quantitative PCR (qPCR) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Significant interaction between AhR and CXCL12, CXCL14, CXCL11, or CXCL2 was not detected.
source: However, significant interaction between AhR and CXCL12, CXCL14, CXCL11, or CXCL2 was not detected (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: BaP significantly induced luciferase activity driven by the CXCL13 promoter containing XRE-like sequence.
source: BaP significantly induced luciferase activity driven by the CXCL13 promoter containing XRE-like sequence; deletion of the XRE-like element, co-incubation with the AhR antagonist α-NF (Wilhelmsson et al., 1994) or transfection of an AhR-specific siRNA significantly reduced luciferase activity (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figures 3C-E.

claim: Deletion of the XRE-like element significantly reduced BaP-induced luciferase activity driven by the CXCL13 promoter.
source: BaP significantly induced luciferase activity driven by the CXCL13 promoter containing XRE-like sequence; deletion of the XRE-like element, co-incubation with the AhR antagonist α-NF (Wilhelmsson et al., 1994) or transfection of an AhR-specific siRNA significantly reduced luciferase activity (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figures 3C-E.

claim: Co-incubation with the AhR antagonist α-NF significantly reduced BaP-induced luciferase activity driven by the CXCL13 promoter.
source: BaP significantly induced luciferase activity driven by the CXCL13 promoter containing XRE-like sequence; deletion of the XRE-like element, co-incubation with the AhR antagonist α-NF (Wilhelmsson et al., 1994) or transfection of an AhR-specific siRNA significantly reduced luciferase activity (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figures 3C-E.

claim: Transfection of an AhR-specific siRNA significantly reduced BaP-induced luciferase activity driven by the CXCL13 promoter.
source: BaP significantly induced luciferase activity driven by the CXCL13 promoter containing XRE-like sequence; deletion of the XRE-like element, co-incubation with the AhR antagonist α-NF (Wilhelmsson et al., 1994) or transfection of an AhR-specific siRNA significantly reduced luciferase activity (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figures 3C-E.

claim: α-NF and siAhR drastically inhibited BaP-caused translocation of AhR to nucleus in 16HBE cells.
source: We reported that α-NF and siAhR drastically inhibited BaP caused translocation of AhR to nucleus in 16HBE cells (Figure 3F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3F-I.

claim: α-NF and siAhR significantly decreased CXCL13 expression in BaP-treated 16HBE cells.
source: These results might explain why α-NF and siAhR significantly decreased CXCL13 expression (Figure 3J) and concentration in the supernatant (Figure 3K) in BaP-treated 16HBE cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR and ELISA data shown in Figures 3J and 3K.

claim: At treatment time points of 120 days, 180 days, and 240 days, Cxcl13-/- mice had much fewer lesions than Cxcl13+/- and Cxcl13+/+ mice.
source: First, tumor nodules in histologic sections of mice upon BaP treatment were analyzed as described (Tan et al., 2013), and the results showed that at treatment time points of 120 days, 180 days, and 240 days, Cxcl13-/- mice had much fewer lesions than Cxcl13+/- and Cxcl13+/+ mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cxcl13-/- mice harbored much fewer lung tumors than Cxcl13+/- and Cxcl13+/+ mice 240 days after BaP treatment.
source: Then, microCT was used to detect visible tumors in mice 240 days after BaP treatment. We found that Cxcl13-/- mice harbored much fewer lung tumors than Cxcl13+/- and Cxcl13+/+ mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microCT data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The tumor volume of Cxcl13-/- mice was significantly smaller than Cxcl13+/- and Cxcl13+/+ mice.
source: Consistent with this observation, the tumor volume of Cxcl13-/- mice was significantly smaller than Cxcl13+/- and Cxcl13+/+ mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by microCT analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In Cxcl13+/+ and Cxcl13-/+ mice, the Cxcl13 serum concentrations were elevated 3 months after BaP treatment, at which time point no tumors were detected.
source: In Cxcl13+/+ and Cxcl13-/+ mice, the Cxcl13 serum concentrations were elevated 3 months after BaP treatment, at which time point no tumors were detected (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The life span of BaP-treated Cxcl13-/- mice was prolonged compared with the Cxcl13+/+ and Cxcl13-/+ mice.
source: Moreover, the life span of BaP-treated Cxcl13-/- mice was prolonged compared with the Cxcl13+/+ and Cxcl13-/+ mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CXCR5 was expressed by the tumor samples but was not significantly higher than in paired normal lung tissues (p=0.089).
source: We tested the expression of CXCR5 in 24 NSCLCs, and found that it was expressed by the tumor samples but was not significantly higher than in paired normal lung tissues (p=0.089; Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In A/J mice treated with BaP, Cxcr5 was slightly up-regulated (p=0.07).
source: In A/J mice treated with BaP, Cxcr5 was slightly up-regulated (p=0.07; Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: BaP-treated Cxcr5+/- mice developed fewer tumors than Cxcr5+/+ mice.
source: We showed that BaP treatment induced lung cancer in Cxcr5+/+ mice (Figure 4H,I). However, BaP-treated Cxcr5+/- mice developed fewer tumors, and BaP-treated Cxcr5-/- mice had much ewer lung tumors (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and microCT data shown in Figures 4H and 4I.

claim: BaP-treated Cxcr5-/- mice had much fewer lung tumors than Cxcr5+/+ and Cxcr5+/- mice.
source: We showed that BaP treatment induced lung cancer in Cxcr5+/+ mice (Figure 4H,I). However, BaP-treated Cxcr5+/- mice developed fewer tumors, and BaP-treated Cxcr5-/- mice had much ewer lung tumors (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and microCT data shown in Figures 4H and 4I.

claim: The tumor volume of Cxcr5-/- mice was significantly lower than Cxcr5+/- and Cxcr5+/+ mice.
source: Consistently, the tumor volume of Cxcr5-/- mice was significantly lower than Cxcr5+/- and Cxcr5+/+ mice (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by microCT analysis data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Cxcr5-/- mice had a prolonged life span compared with the wild-type and Cxcr5+/- mice.
source: Furthermore, Cxcr5-/- mice had a prolonged life span compared with the wild-type and Cxcr5+/- mice (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: CXCR5 is critical for BaP-induced lung cancer.
source: These results demonstrate that CXCR5 is also critical for BaP-induced lung cancer.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Cxcr5 knockout mouse data showing reduced tumor burden and prolonged survival.

claim: There was a significant increase in Cd68+ macrophages in the lung tumor samples from BaP-treated A/J mice.
source: Flow cytometry analysis showed a significant increase in Cd68+ macrophages in the lung tumor samples from BaP-treated A/J mice (Figure 5A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: 94.7% of Cd68+ macrophages in mouse lung tumors strongly expressed Cxcr5.
source: We found that 94.7% of these macrophages strongly expressed Cxcr5 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: B cells and T cells were not enriched in the tumor microenvironment of BaP-treated mice.
source: However, B cells and T cells were not enriched in the tumor microenvironment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD68+ macrophages were enriched in human lung tumor tissues.
source: Moreover, CD68+ macrophages were enriched in human lung tumor tissues revealed by IHC (Figure 5C) and immunofluorescence assays (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 5C and 5E.

claim: THP-1 macrophage cell line expressed high levels of CXCR5 and CD68.
source: The Tamm–Horsfall protein (THP-1) macrophage cell line also expressed high levels of CXCR5 and CD68 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: THP-1 cells induced the migration of A549-Luc cells and H1975 cells in a trans-well migration assay.
source: In a trans-well migration assay, THP-1 cells induced the migration of A549-Luciferase (Luc) cells and H1975 cells from the upper chamber to the lower chamber (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-well migration assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Stable transfection of CXCL13 into A549-Luc cells significantly enhanced the migration activity induced by THP-1 cells.
source: Stable transfection of CXCL13 into A549-Luc cells (designated A549-Luc-CXCL13 cells) significantly enhanced the migration activity, which was antagonized by an anti-CXCR5 antibody (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-well migration assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: An anti-CXCR5 antibody antagonized the enhanced migration activity of A549-Luc-CXCL13 cells induced by THP-1 cells.
source: Stable transfection of CXCL13 into A549-Luc cells (designated A549-Luc-CXCL13 cells) significantly enhanced the migration activity, which was antagonized by an anti-CXCR5 antibody (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-well migration assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Addition of CXCL13 to THP-1 cells enhanced the migration of H1975 cells.
source: Addition of CXCL13 to THP-1 cells enhanced the migration of H1975 cells, while an anti-CXCR5 antibody inhibited this effect (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-well migration assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: An anti-CXCR5 antibody inhibited the CXCL13-enhanced migration of H1975 cells induced by THP-1 cells.
source: Addition of CXCL13 to THP-1 cells enhanced the migration of H1975 cells, while an anti-CXCR5 antibody inhibited this effect (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-well migration assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: A549-Luc-CXCL13 cells significantly increased the tumor burden in NOD/SCID mice compared with A549-Luc cells.
source: We showed that compared with the A549-Luc cells, the A549-Luc-CXCL13 cells significantly increased the tumor burden in the recipient mice (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: Tail vein-injection of THP-1 cells increased the volume of tumors formed by the A549-Luc-CXCL13 cells.
source: Furthermore, tail vein-injection of THP-1 cells increased the volume of tumors formed by the A549-Luc-CXCL13 cells (Figure 5G,H)
evidence: This claim is supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: Tail vein-injection of THP-1 cells caused obvious metastases to the left lung of mice bearing A549-Luc-CXCL13 tumors.
source: and caused obvious metastases to the left lung of the mice (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: 436 genes were found to be associated with CXCL13 (a coefficient >0.5 or <−0.5) in a whole genome gene expression assay of eight HPR patients.
source: To identify these factors, a whole genome gene expression assay was performed in the eight patients (Figure 1A), and 436 genes were found to be associated with CXCL13 (a coefficient >0.5 or <−0.5; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray data analysis.

claim: CXCL13-associated genes were enriched in cytokine-cytokine receptor interactions, the Wnt signaling pathway, the calcium signaling pathway, and others.
source: These genes were enriched in cytokine-cytokine receptor interactions, the Wnt signaling pathway, the calcium signaling pathway, and others (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Among the secretion-related genes, MMP12, SPP1, and MMP7 had the highest coefficient values for interacting with CXCL13.
source: Among the secretion-related genes, MMP12, secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1), which encodes a macrophage-secreted cytokine SPP1 or osteopontin (Kohri et al., 1992), and MMP7 had the highest coefficient values for interacting with CXCL13 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The expression of SPP1 was the highest among 11 secretion-related genes tested in THP-1 cells.
source: We tested 11 secretion-related genes in THP-1 cells, and found that the expression of SPP1 was the highest (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CXCL13 treatment significantly increased SPP1 concentrations in the supernatant of THP-1 cells.
source: In THP-1 cells, CXCL13 treatment significantly increased SPP1 concentrations in the supernatant (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Addition of CXCL13 to THP-1 cells enhanced the migration of H1975 cells, while SPP1 silencing in THP-1 cells attenuated this effect.
source: In trans-well assays, the addition of CXCL13 to THP-1 cells in the lower chamber enhanced the migration of H1975 cells, while SPP1 silencing by siSPP1 in THP-1 cells attenuated this effect (Figure 6E, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-well migration assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Transfection of CXCL13 into A549 cells increased their migration activity, while SPP1 silencing in THP-1 cells inhibited A549-CXCL13 cell migration.
source: Transfection of CXCL13 into A549 cells increased their migration activity, while SPP1 silencing in THP-1 cells inhibited A549-CXCL13 cell migration (Figure 6E, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-well migration assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In BaP-treated A/J mice, the Spp1 serum concentration was significantly increased.
source: In BaP-treated A/J mice, the Spp1 serum concentration was significantly increased (Figure 6F)
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The tumor samples from BaP-treated mice showed significantly increased Spp1 IHC staining compared with the control mice.
source: and the tumor samples showed significantly increased Spp1 IHC staining compared with the control mice (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Cd68 positive macrophages were strongly stained by Spp1, whereas Ttf1-positive lung cancer cells were only weakly stained positive for Spp1.
source: By IHC assay, we found that Cd68 positive macrophages were also strongly stained by Spp1, whereas Ttf1-positive lung cancer cells were only weakly stained positive for Spp1 (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Cd68-positive macrophages were the main source of Spp1 in mice exposed to BaP.
source: These results indicate that Cd68-positive macrophages were the main source of Spp1 in mice exposed to BaP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the IHC and immunofluorescence data showing predominant Spp1 expression in Cd68-positive macrophages.

claim: In BaP-treated A/J mice, the expression of E-Cadherin was down-regulated, while N-Cadherin, Vimentin, Slug and Snail were up-regulated.
source: We tested the epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT) phenotypes that are associated with cancer progression and metastasis (Kalluri and Weinberg, 2009) in tumor samples from the BaP-treated A/J mice, and found that the expression of E-Cadherin was down-regulated, while N-Cadherin, Vimentin, Slug and Snail were up-regulated (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At protein level, E-Cadherin was down-regulated, while N-Cadherin and Vimentin were up-regulated in the tumors of BaP-treated mice.
source: At protein level, E-Cadherin was down-regulated, while N-Cadherin and Vimentin were up-regulated in the tumors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The nuclear β-catenin levels were increased in the tumor samples from BaP-treated A/J mice.
source: We showed that the nuclear β-catenin levels were increased in the tumor samples from A/J mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SPP1 overexpression decreased the cytoplasmic expression but increased the nuclear expression of β-catenin in A549 cells.
source: We found that SPP1 overexpression decreased the cytoplasmic expression but increased the nuclear expression of β-catenin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H,I.

claim: SPP1 overexpression in cancer cells led to the down-regulation of E-Cadherin and up-regulation of N-Cadherin and Slug at both the mRNA and protein levels.
source: SPP1 overexpression in cancer cells led to the down-regulation of E-Cadherin and up-regulation of N-Cadherin and Slug at both the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J,K)
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J,K.

claim: SPP1 overexpression led to up-regulation of Vimentin and Snail at the mRNA level.
source: and up-regulation of Vimentin and Snail at the mRNA level (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J.

claim: SPP1 may transactivate β-catenin to induce an EMT in BaP-treated mice.
source: These results suggest that SPP1 may transactivate β-catenin to induce an EMT in BaP-treated mice.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data showing SPP1's effects on β-catenin and EMT markers.

claim: BaP induced lung epithelial cells to secret CXCL13, which recruited tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and induced SPP1 production.
source: BaP induced lung epithelial cells to secret CXCL13 (Figure 2), which recruited tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and induced SPP1 production (Figure 5, 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data from the study.

claim: SPP1 activated β-catenin by facilitating its translocation to the nucleus and promoted an EMT, leading to the progression of lung cancer.
source: SPP1 activated β-catenin by facilitating its translocation to the nucleus and promoted an EMT, leading to the progression of lung cancer (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing SPP1's effects on β-catenin localization and EMT markers.

claim: CXCL13-CXCR5 signaling was required for PAH-induced lung cancer.
source: CXCL13-CXCR5 signaling was required for PAH-induced lung cancer, because knockdown of Cxcl13 or Cxcr5 attenuated BaP-induced lung cancer in mice (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by knockout mouse experimental data.

claim: The ubiquitous carcinogen BaP may induce tumor-promoting inflammation to facilitate the invasive growth and metastasis of lung cancer.
source: These results suggest that the ubiquitous carcinogen BaP may induce tumor-promoting inflammation to facilitate the invasive growth and metastasis of lung cancer, shedding new insights into the carcinogenic mechanisms of air pollution.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: CXCL13 may be associated with lung cancer risk in smokers.
source: CXCL13 may be associated with lung cancer risk in smokers (Shiels et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: High CXCL13 expression was associated with advanced stage cancer and poor prognosis.
source: Moreover, high CXCL13 expression was associated with advanced stage cancer and poor prognosis (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data analysis shown in Figure 2 (likely referring to Figure 1K and 1L).

claim: The serum concentration of CXCL13 was elevated in mice before the emergence of detectable lung tumor by microCT.
source: Furthermore, the serum concentration of CXCL13 was elevated in mice before the emergence of detectable lung tumor by microCT (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA and microCT data.

claim: CXCL13 may represent a biomarker for early diagnosis of lung cancer.
source: suggesting that this chemokine may represent a biomarker for early diagnosis, which warrants further investigation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation of early CXCL13 elevation.

claim: PAHs cause mutations in TP53 and K-RAS, resulting in uncontrolled cell growth.
source: PAHs are key carcinogens in air pollution and tobacco smoke (Huang et al., 2014; Hecht, 2012), and cause mutations in TP53 and K-RAS, resulting in uncontrolled cell growth (Hecht, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: CXCL13 was a direct target of AhR.
source: We found that CXCL13 was a direct target of AhR (Figure 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP and luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: An anti-CXCR5 antibody significantly inhibited lung cancer cell migration.
source: while an anti-CXCR5 antibody significantly inhibited lung cancer cell migration (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by trans-well migration assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: SPP1 activates β–catenin and is regulated by this transcription factor.
source: Using a whole -genome gene expression array (Figure 6), we discovered that TAMs secreted SPP1, which activates β–catenin and is regulated by this transcription factor (Robertson and Chellaiah, 2010; El-Tanani et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research and the study's gene expression data.

claim: SPP1 induced the nuclear localization and activation of β–catenin in epithelial and cancer cells, resulting in an EMT phenotype.
source: SPP1 induced the nuclear localization and activation of β–catenin in epithelial and cancer cells, resulting in an EMT phenotype (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–K.

claim: SPP1-β–catenin could form a positive feedback loop to promote EMT and lung cancer progression.
source: However, our results suggested that SPP1-β–catenin could form a positive feedback loop to promote EMT and lung cancer progression.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: CXCL13 was shown to be able to induce an EMT in breast cancer via RANKL and Src activation.
source: CXCL13 was shown to be able to induce an EMT in breast cancer via RANKL and Src activation (Biswas et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: BaP or CXCL13 treatment or SPP1 overexpression in lung epithelial or cancer cells did not up-regulate RANKL or Src.
source: We found that BaP or CXCL13 treatment or SPP1 overexpression in lung epithelial or cancer cells did not up-regulate RANKL or Src (data not shown)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data not shown in the manuscript.

claim: CXCL13 may induce an EMT via different mechanisms in different settings.
source: suggesting that CXCL13 may induce an EMT via different mechanisms in different settings.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on comparison with previous research.

claim: CCL20 is induced by nicotine-derived nitrosaminoketone and is overexpressed in smoker lung cancers and inversely associated with prognosis.
source: For example, CCL20 is induced by another important carcinogen in tobacco smoke, nicotine-derived nitrosaminoketone, and is overexpressed in smoker lung cancers and inversely associated with prognosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Wang et al., 2015).

claim: CCL20 promotes lung cancer cell proliferation and migration.
source: CCL20 promotes lung cancer cell proliferation and migration (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: CXCL12 and CCR7 regulate the metastasis of breast cancers and NSCLCs.
source: CXCL12 and CCR7 regulate the metastasis of breast cancers and NSCLCs (Phillips et al., 2003; Müller et al., 2001; Takanami, 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CXCL1/2 enhance cell survival and promote chemoresistance.
source: while CXCL1/2 enhance cell survival and promote chemoresistance (Acharyya et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: CXCL13 is overexpressed in breast cancer.
source: CXCL13 is overexpressed in breast cancer (Panse et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: CXCL13 mediates prostate cancer cell proliferation.
source: and mediates prostate cancer cell proliferation (El-Haibi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: DEX reduces lung tumor multiplicities in the tobacco smoke-exposed and non-exposed mice.
source: It reduces lung tumor multiplicities in the tobacco smoke-exposed and non-exposed mice (Witschi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: DEX inhibited CXCL13 production by epithelial cells and SPP1 production by TAMs.
source: We showed that DEX inhibited CXCL13 production by epithelial cells and SPP1 production by TAMs (Figure 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: DEX inhibited the EMT in BaP-treated mice.
source: inhibited the EMT (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: DEX reduced the tumor burden and prolonged the life span of BaP-treated mice.
source: reduced the tumor burden and prolonged the life span of the mice (Figure 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.
